newsitem.title: CHILE: Ruling coalition wins local elections in Chile.
newsitem.headline: Ruling coalition wins local elections in Chile.

text.p: President Eduardo Frei's centre-left coalition won Chilean municipal elections by a wide margin on Sunday, but an alliance of two conservative parties made major gains, early results showed.
With 54 percent of the ballots counted, the four parties in the governing coalition known as the Concertacion won 56 percent of the vote, compared to 34 percent for the rightist Union for Chile.

The results, announced by Deputy Interior Secretary Belisario Velasco, showed continued support for Chile's ruling coalition, which has governed over a prosperous economy and a stable country since the military left power in 1990.

But support grew sharply for the rightist alliance, made up of two pro-business parties with close ties to the military that appeared to be winning mayoral seats in major cities like La Serena and Vina del Mar and many large Santiago suburbs.
"This is our night. The centre-right has made a spectacular advance all over the country," said Senator Sebastian Pinera of the rightist National Renewal party.
The opposition alliance won 28 percent of the vote in the last municipal polls in 1992 and opinion polls had tipped it to win only about 30 percent this year.
The poll was the first direct election of mayors and councillors in Chile's 341 cities and towns. Until now the mayors had been chosen by the councillors.
Frei's Christian Democratic Party alone was holding at 25 percent -- below expectations, and down from the 29 percent it won in the 1992 municipal elections.
But its three coalition partners all raised their shares, including the leftist Party for Democracy (PPD) and the Socialists, which together stood at 23 percent.

Christian Democratic leaders denied the results would bring a tilt to the left in the Concertacion coalition, which Frei has succeeded in holding together despite political crises and rivalries since taking office in 1994.

"Our party will continue to be the axis of the Concertacion. We consider the results satisfactory...although there has been some erosion (of the party's support)," said Christian Democratic Party president Alejandro Foxley.
But the results looked likely to strengthen the position of Public Works Minister Ricardo Lagos of the PPD over his Christian Democratic rivals for the coalition's 1999 presidential nomination.
Polls show that Lagos, a leading opponent of military rule by Gen. Augusto Pinochet in the 1980s, is the only politician in Chile more popular than Frei, who cannot seek reeelction.
The Christian Democratic mayor of Santiago, Jaime Ravinet, appeared headed for easy reelection although with a smaller margin than many expected, about 40 percent.

The big losers appeared to be the hardline Communists, who won only about four percent, and a once-important rightist party known as the Progressive Centre-Centre, which stayed out of the Union for Chile and got only three percent of the vote.
